facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered by Edwin Delfs in 1957 in the Morrison Formation near Canon City, Colorado.
facts.quote: The holotype of Eutretauranosuchus delfsi was discovered by Edwin Delfs in 1957 among remains recovered from the Morrison Formation in Canon City, Colorado.

facts.statement: Charles Mook first described the species in detail in 1967.
facts.quote: It was first described in detail by Charles Mook in 1967.

facts.statement: The genus name refers to the animal's "doubly pierced palate".
facts.quote: The name Eutretauranosuchus was given by Delfs upon its discovery in reference to its "doubly pierced palate".

facts.statement: The species name *delfsi* honors the discoverer Edwin Delfs.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen was named E. delfsi by Mook in tribute to Delfs.

facts.statement: The fossil record includes an almost-complete skull and some limb bones.
facts.quote: The fossil remains consisted of an almost-complete skull as well as some limb bones.

facts.statement: It is an extinct genus of goniopholidid crocodyliform.
facts.quote: Eutretauranosuchus is an extinct genus of goniopholidid crocodyliform.

facts.statement: Its skull is elongated and platyrostral with broadened nasals and a flattened innerfenestral bar.
facts.quote: Characteristics of E. delfi skulls include an elongated and platyrostral skull, posterolateral depressions on the alveolar maxillary process, minimal lateral undulation of the tooth row (maxillary), broadened nasals located anteriorly to the prefrontals, a lack of contact between the nasals and external nares, a flattened and broad innerfenestral bar with rims that are raised along the supratemporal fenestra, and a nasopharyngeal septum formed by the anterior divergence of the vomeral processes.

facts.statement: The rectangular lacrimal bone is twice as long as it is wide.
facts.quote: The lacrimal bone is rectangular and in dorsal view has an anteroposterior length that is two times its width.

facts.statement: The quadratojugal bone has a pitted ventral region that creates a characteristic indentation.
facts.quote: The quadratojugal has two regions: a smaller dorsal part that lacks dermal pitting, and a larger ventral region that is pitted and forms the bottom half of the infratemporal process, creating a significant indentation that is considered characteristic of this genus.

facts.statement: Specimens are estimated to have weighed between 50 and 60 kg.
facts.quote: Preserved specimens indicate Eutretauranosuchus are moderately sized with an average estimated weight of 50–60 kg.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests it was carnivorous, feeding on insects, fish, small reptiles, mammals, and dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The size and length of Goniopholididae specimens found in the Morrison Formation, as well as striated teeth, support the hypothesis that Eutretauranosuchus were carnivorous, feeding on prey such as insects, fish, small reptiles, mammals and dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Chemical analysis of its teeth suggests a diet focused on fish.
facts.quote: Eutretauranosuchus exhibited low enamel δ44/40Ca values, suggesting a piscivorous diet.

facts.statement: It is categorized as a semi-aquatic animal.
facts.quote: Goniopholidid crocodilians, including Eutretauranosuchus, are widely categorized as semi-aquatic forms.

facts.statement: Fossils are found in the Morrison Formation in Colorado and Wyoming.
facts.quote: Eutretauranosuchus is currently known from specimens found in the Upper Jurassic Dry Mesa Dinosaur Quarry in Canon City, Colorado; the Brushy Basin Member in Western Colorado; and the Bone Cabin Quarry site in Wyoming—all of which are parts of the Morrison Formation.

facts.statement: It lived in estuarine and freshwater environments.
facts.quote: Specimens from this group are often found in estuarine and freshwater deposits.

facts.statement: It lived between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (154.8 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: *Eutretauranosuchus delfsi* is the only known species in the genus.
facts.quote: E. delfsi is the only known species within the genus.

facts.statement: Related genera include *Amphicotylus*, *Goniopholis*, *Sunosuchus*, and *Calsoyasuchus*.
facts.quote: Other genera of Goniopholididae include Amphicotylus, Goniopholis, Sunosuchus, and Calsoyasuchus.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests the additional nasal opening described by Mook was an illusion caused by an hourglass-shaped choana.
facts.quote: Recent findings suggest that Mook's original description of an additional nasal opening was incorrect and that this opening was part of an elongated choana that is extremely constricted medially by the expansion of the palatines, giving the illusion of a separate anteriorly located opening due to its hourglass-shape—as is commonly described in other E. delfsi, Amphicotylus lucasii and A. gilmorei specimens.

facts.statement: Some analyses place it closer to *Pholidosaurus* and dyrosaurids within a larger clade including *Bernissartia* and eusuchians.
facts.quote: Alternatively, phylogenetic assessment by J.R. Foster in 2006 considers Eutretauranosuchus to be most closely related to Pholidosaurus and dyrosauridae, and belonging to a larger clade that includes Bernissartia, Eusuchians and Goniopholis.

facts.statement: A crest on dorsal osteoderms suggests epaxial muscles attached differently than in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: The anteroposteriorly located crest on the ventral surfaces of Goniopholididae dorsal osteoderms has been hypothesized to be evidence that the epaxial musculature attached medially to a single paravertebral osteoderm, which is different from the three groups of epaxial musculature that attach to separate osteoderms in extant crocodylians.
